1.title: LORE knowledge mode — standard-text consensus (not source-verified) (tier K)

2.title: LORE knowledge mode — exam convention (PYQ keys) (tier K)

K1.text: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous, elongated superficial veins; in CEAP they are veins **≥3 mm** in diameter measured standing.

K2.text: The **great saphenous vein (GSV)** system is the most commonly affected, and **saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) incompetence** is the most common site of reflux.

K3.text: **Duplex ultrasound (colour Doppler)** is the investigation of choice for varicose veins.

K4.text: **Brodie–Trendelenburg test** detects SFJ incompetence; **Perthes test** checks deep vein patency.

K5.text: **Endovenous thermal ablation** (radiofrequency or laser) is the current first-line treatment for truncal saphenous reflux; ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy is next, and open surgery is used if both are unsuitable.

K6.text: **Trendelenburg operation** = flush ligation of the GSV at the SFJ with ligation of all its tributaries.

K7.text: The GSV is stripped only to just below the knee to avoid **saphenous nerve** injury.

K8.text: Short saphenous vein surgery risks the **sural nerve**.

K9.text: **Venous ulcers** occur in the **gaiter area**, most commonly just above the **medial malleolus**.

K10.text: Compression for a venous ulcer requires an **ABPI ≥0.8** to exclude significant arterial disease.

K11.text: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous and elongated superficial veins with incompetent valves.

K12.text: In the CEAP classification, varicose veins (C2) are subcutaneous veins **≥3 mm** in diameter in the upright position.

K13.text: Telangiectasias (<1 mm) and reticular veins (1–3 mm) form CEAP class C1.

K14.text: **Great (long) saphenous vein:** begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, runs **anterior to the medial malleolus**, ascends on the medial side of leg and thigh, and joins the **femoral vein** at the SFJ through the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis) inferolateral to the **pubic tubercle**.

K15.text: The GSV is the **longest vein** in the body.

K16.text: The **saphenous nerve** accompanies the GSV in the leg below the knee.

K17.text: Tributaries at the SFJ include the **superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac and superficial external pudendal** veins, along with the deep external pudendal vein.

K18.text: **Short (small) saphenous vein:** begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, runs **behind the lateral malleolus**, and usually joins the **popliteal vein** at the saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ) in the popliteal fossa.

K19.text: The **sural nerve** accompanies the short saphenous vein.

K20.text: The level of the SPJ is variable, so it is marked by duplex before surgery.

K21.text: **Perforating veins** connect superficial to deep veins, and their valves normally allow flow only from superficial to deep.

K22.text: **Cockett** — Medial lower leg/ankle; connect the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins

K23.text: **Boyd** — Medial leg just below the knee

K26.text: Current anatomical nomenclature replaces these eponyms with descriptive names (e.g. posterior tibial perforators for Cockett).

K27.text: **Primary varicose veins** (most common) arise from intrinsic weakness of the vein wall and valves without a deep venous cause.

K28.text: **Secondary varicose veins** follow deep vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic), pelvic masses or pregnancy obstructing venous outflow, arteriovenous fistula, or congenital malformations such as **Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome**.

K29.text: Risk factors include **female sex, pregnancy, family history, increasing age, prolonged standing, and obesity**.

K30.text: In pregnancy, **progesterone**-mediated venous dilatation and pressure of the gravid uterus on pelvic veins both contribute.

K31.text: Congenital absence of valves is a rare cause.

K32.text: Valve incompetence allows **reflux** (retrograde flow) of blood from deep to superficial veins or down the superficial trunks.

K33.text: Normally the **calf muscle pump** lowers venous pressure in the leg during walking.

K34.text: With reflux or deep obstruction, pressure fails to fall on walking, causing **ambulatory venous hypertension**.

K35.text: Sustained venous hypertension causes capillary leak of fluid, red cells and fibrinogen, with leukocyte trapping and inflammation, leading to oedema, skin changes and ulceration.

K36.text: **Haemosiderin** from extravasated red cells causes the brown skin pigmentation.

K37.text: Symptoms include **aching, heaviness, itching, cramps and ankle swelling**, worse after prolonged standing and at the end of the day, and relieved by **leg elevation**.

K38.text: Many patients present for cosmetic reasons with no symptoms.

K39.text: Skin changes of chronic venous insufficiency include **pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche** and **corona phlebectatica**.

K40.text: **Lipodermatosclerosis** is induration and fibrosis of skin and subcutaneous fat of the lower leg, giving an **"inverted champagne bottle"** leg shape.

K41.text: **Atrophie blanche** is white, scarred skin with dilated capillary dots, and marks a high risk of ulceration.

K42.text: **Corona phlebectatica** is a fan of small intradermal veins around the ankle and foot.

K43.text: **Saphena varix** is a dilatation of the GSV at the SFJ that disappears on lying down, has a **cough impulse** and a **fluid thrill on tapping**, and is a differential for **femoral hernia**.

K44.text: **Brodie–Trendelenburg test** — Leg elevated, veins emptied, SFJ compressed, patient stands. Rapid filling from above on release of pressure = **SFJ incompetence**; filling with pressure still on = **perforator** incompetence

K45.text: **Tourniquet test (multiple tourniquet)** — Tourniquets at different levels localise the level of the incompetent perforator

K46.text: **Perthes test** — Tourniquet applied, patient walks/exercises; veins empty if **deep veins are patent** and perforators competent; increased pain and distension suggest **deep vein obstruction**

K47.text: **Schwartz (tap) test** — Tap at a lower varicosity felt at the SFJ indicates a continuous column of blood with incompetent valves

K48.text: **Cough impulse (Morrissey's)** — Impulse at the SFJ on coughing indicates SFJ incompetence

K49.text: **Fegan's test** — Palpable fascial defects mark the sites of incompetent perforators

K50.text: **Pratt's test** — Uses bandages to show the sites of incompetent perforators

K51.text: A positive Perthes test (deep vein obstruction) is a **contraindication** to superficial vein ligation or stripping, because superficial veins are then acting as collaterals.

K52.text: **Duplex ultrasound** is the **investigation of choice**, showing the anatomy of reflux, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency.

K53.text: Reflux on duplex is usually defined as retrograde flow lasting **>0.5 seconds** in superficial veins and **>1 second** in the femoral and popliteal veins.

K54.text: Hand-held Doppler can detect junctional reflux at the bedside but has been superseded by duplex.

K55.text: **Venography** is not routine and is reserved for complex deep venous disease or planned deep venous intervention.

K56.text: Photoplethysmography and air plethysmography measure venous refilling time and global venous function.

K57.text: **ABPI** should be measured before compression therapy to exclude arterial disease.

K58.text: C0 — No visible or palpable signs of venous disease

K62.text: C4 — Skin changes: C4a pigmentation or eczema; C4b lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche; C4c corona phlebectatica

K65.text: CEAP stands for **Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological**.

K66.text: The **2020 CEAP revision** added C4c (corona phlebectatica) and the "r" modifier for recurrent varicose veins (C2r) and recurrent ulcer (C6r).

K67.text: The Venous Clinical Severity Score (VCSS) is used to track severity and response to treatment.

K68.text: Conservative measures are leg elevation, exercise, weight reduction and avoiding prolonged standing.

K69.text: **Graduated compression stockings** relieve symptoms and are used when intervention is unsuitable or declined, in pregnancy, and after treatment.

K70.text: Compression is **contraindicated** in significant peripheral arterial disease (ABPI <0.8).

K71.text: NICE advises against offering compression hosiery as treatment for symptomatic varicose veins when interventional treatment is suitable.

K72.text: **Endothermal ablation** — **radiofrequency ablation (RFA)** or **endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)** — is first-line.

K73.text: **Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy** is offered if endothermal ablation is unsuitable.

K74.text: **Open surgery** (ligation and stripping) is offered if neither is suitable.

K75.text: Endothermal ablation is done under **tumescent local anaesthesia**, which also protects surrounding tissue from heat.

K76.text: Endovenous heat-induced thrombosis (**EHIT**), thrombus extending from the ablated vein into the deep vein, is a specific complication of thermal ablation.

K77.text: Non-thermal, non-tumescent options include **cyanoacrylate glue** closure and mechanochemical ablation (MOCA).

K78.text: Sclerotherapy injects a sclerosant that damages the endothelium so the vein fibroses and closes.

K79.text: Common sclerosants are **sodium tetradecyl sulphate (STS)** and **polidocanol**.

K80.text: **Foam sclerotherapy** (Tessari technique, mixing sclerosant with air) displaces blood and is more effective than liquid in larger veins.

K81.text: Liquid sclerotherapy is best for telangiectasias, reticular veins and small residual varicosities.

K82.text: Complications of sclerotherapy include skin pigmentation, skin necrosis from extravasation, thrombophlebitis, DVT and, with foam, transient visual disturbance or neurological events.

K83.text: **Trendelenburg operation:** flush ligation of the GSV at the SFJ with ligation of all tributaries, through a groin incision.

K84.text: The GSV is then **stripped** from the groin to just below the knee.

K85.text: Stripping below the knee is avoided because of the risk of **saphenous nerve** injury.

K86.text: **Multiple stab avulsions (ambulatory phlebectomy)** remove residual tributary varicosities.

K87.text: Short saphenous incompetence is treated by **SPJ ligation** in the popliteal fossa, with risk to the **sural nerve** and the common peroneal nerve.

K88.text: Incompetent perforators can be ligated by **subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS)** or the older open Linton procedure.

K89.text: Surgery for superficial varicose veins is contraindicated when the deep veins are occluded.

K90.text: **Multilayer (four-layer) compression bandaging** is the mainstay of venous ulcer treatment.

K91.text: An **Unna boot** is a zinc-oxide-impregnated compression dressing.

K92.text: Correcting superficial venous reflux by early endovenous ablation speeds ulcer healing and reduces recurrence (EVRA trial).

K93.text: A non-healing ulcer with an atypical edge should be biopsied to exclude **Marjolin's ulcer** (squamous cell carcinoma).

K94.text: **Haemorrhage** from a ruptured varix, controlled by leg elevation and direct pressure.

K98.text: **Marjolin's ulcer** (squamous cell carcinoma) in a long-standing ulcer.

K99.text: Periostitis, calcification of the veins, and ankle stiffness (equinus) in long-standing disease.

K100.text: **Saphenous nerve** injury after below-knee GSV stripping or ablation, causing numbness on the medial leg.

K101.text: **Sural nerve** injury with short saphenous surgery or ablation.

K102.text: Haematoma, wound infection, groin lymphocele/lymphatic leak, and DVT.

K103.text: Injury to the femoral vein or artery at the SFJ is a rare but serious surgical complication.

K104.text: **Recurrence** after surgery is common, and **neovascularisation** at the ligated SFJ is a leading cause.

K119.text: PYQs have expected **Trendelenburg operation with stripping** as the treatment of varicose veins with SFJ incompetence; current practice (NICE) is **endothermal ablation first-line**, then foam sclerotherapy, then surgery.

K120.text: Brodie–Trendelenburg is a test for **SFJ incompetence**; Perthes is a test for **deep vein patency**; do not swap them.

K121.text: The "Trendelenburg test" (varicose veins), the "Trendelenburg operation" (SFJ ligation), the Trendelenburg position and the Trendelenburg sign (hip abductor weakness) are different things.

K122.text: Dodd perforators are in the **thigh** (Hunter's canal region) while Cockett perforators are at the **ankle/lower leg**; Boyd is just **below the knee**.

K123.text: The GSV runs **in front of the medial malleolus**; the SSV runs **behind the lateral malleolus**.

K124.text: **Saphena varix** vs **femoral hernia**: both have a cough impulse, but a saphena varix has a fluid thrill on tapping and empties on lying down.

K125.text: Before stripping or ligation, deep vein patency must be confirmed (Perthes or duplex), because in deep vein occlusion the superficial veins are the collateral outflow.

K126.text: Sclerosant answers: **sodium tetradecyl sulphate** is the classic answer; polidocanol is an equally accepted modern agent.
